[PAPER_0016, relevance_score=0.279] Across two experiments, participants listened to tonal chord sequences that were either unchanged (high temporal coherence) or were scrambled to produce increasingly incoherent sequences (medium and low temporal coherence) based on IDyOM's predictions. For each sequence, participants then completed an intonation discrimination task for the target chord, which was either in or out of tune relative to the preceding context. It was predicted that temporally incoherent (scrambled) chord sequences would slow the speed and accuracy of processing, thereby providing evidence to support a functional interpretation of tonal-harmonic processing (H1).

[PAPER_0017, relevance_score=0.318] Sears et al. (2019) also reported significant effects of musical training in a priming experiment that employed examples of expectancy violation derived from real instances of tonal music. Thus, the participants selected for this study were also derived from two groups: musicians in at least the second year of their university studies, and general participants with less than one year of reported formal training. Given their greater training in (or exposure to) tonal harmony, it was predicted that musicians would be faster and more accurate in their responses than general participants (H2).

[PAPER_0019, relevance_score=0.377] It was predicted that controlling for task difficulty would mitigate the effects of musical training across the experiment (H3), indicating harmonic priming effects are more likely to reflect implicit rather than explicit learning strategies (Bigand, 2003). Finally, exploratory mixed-effects regression analyses simulate the obtained priming data from Experiments 1 and 2 to examine the impact of several possible predictors of stimulus coherence.

All participants also provided informed consent, and the study was certified for ethical compliance by the Texas Tech University Institutional Review Board (IRB2019-97).

[PAPER_0112, relevance_score=0.341] After controlling for potential differences in task difficulty, it was predicted that Experiment 2 would replicate the findings for the temporal coherence manipulation from Experiment 1, but the effect of musical training would no longer be significant for any of the dependent measures (H3). Finally, the simulations examined whether alternative measures of temporal coherence might better account for the observed priming effects.

As expected, correct RTs in both experiments revealed an ascending staircase from the high to the low coherence conditions, suggesting a processing advantage for the unscrambled sequences, a processing cost for the scrambled sequences, or both.

To examine the relationships between the selected predictors and the behavioral responses from musicians and general participants for each stimulus (N = 48), log-transformed, correct RTs and logit transformations of the proportion of correct responses were averaged (or aggregated) across participants from in-tune trials. As shown in Table 1, intercorrelations between the selected predictors and the behavioral responses revealed moderate-to-strong correlations between the information-theoretic predictors produced by IDyOM and the correct RTs from both groups across both experiments.

[PAPER_0096, relevance_score=0.336] Bartlett's test of sphericity, χ2(15) = 139.39, p < .001, further indicated that these correlations were sufficiently large to justify dimensionality reduction as a preceding step in the regression analysis pipeline.

A principal component analysis (PCA) was conducted on the six predictors estimated by IDyOM with orthogonal rotation (varimax).

[PAPER_0099, relevance_score=0.392] Following PCA, mixed-effects regression models were fitted for response accuracies and correct RTs from in-tune trials in both experiments for musicians and general participants. LMMs for both dependent measures included fixed effects for the three principal components and crossed random intercepts for participants and musical stimuli. Models were fit using backward stepwise selection using the buildmer package (Voeten, 2020).

[PAPER_0100, relevance_score=0.396] Finally, unstandardized parameter estimates (B) were calculated using the package lme4 (Bates et al., 2015), and standardized beta coefficients (β) were calculated using the package effectsize (Ben-Schachar et al., 2020).

As shown in Table 3, all generalized linear mixed-effects models (GLMMs) for the accuracy of responses from in-tune trials initially retained PC1, harmonic surprisal, with similar coefficients for both groups across all experiments.

All data for Experiment 2 were collected in 2020-2021. The experimental design, hypotheses, and analysis plan were separately preregistered on the Open Science Framework (see https://osf.io/wx8f3), and the stimuli, behavioral data, and analysis scripts are available for download at https://osf.io/6anvs/.

[PAPER_0089, relevance_score=0.283] Method

Each of the selected measures predicted the target melodic tone, chord, or sequence for each stimulus. For the information-theoretic predictors estimated by IDyOM, the LTM was trained to predict each chord and melodic pitch event in the harmonic and melodic representations using the BCMH corpus. For D, a normal probability distribution function was fit to the melodic interval sizes encountered in the upper-voice melodies from the complete digitized corpus of Bach chorales (N = 371; http://kern.ccarh.org/).

[PAPER_0095, relevance_score=0.302] To address this issue, Table 2 presents the intercorrelations between the selected predictors. Alternative measures, K and D, were excluded due to poor performance in the preceding correlational analysis. As expected, target surprisal, IC, and sequence surprisal, Hm, were strongly correlated across both harmonic and melodic representations (r range: .57-.78). By comparison, correlations involving target uncertainty, H, were generally weaker (r range: .29-.56).

[PAPER_0097, relevance_score=0.320] The Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin (KMO) measure verified the sampling adequacy for the analysis, KMO = .77, and all KMO values for individual predictors were larger than .59, which is above the acceptable limit of .5. Following PCA, two components had eigenvalues over Kaiser's criterion of 1 and in combination explained 77% of the variance.
